title: Article: storing trillions of messages
objective: Follow Discord's write-up of how it stores trillions of messages: hot partitions, request coalescing, and moving its biggest cluster to a new database.

sources.title: Discord Blog: How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages (Bo Ingram, 6 Mar 2023): "We partition our messages by the channel they're sent in, along with a bucket, which is a static time window."

simplifies: Simplified from Discord's own article; the dates are the ones it gives. Discord's database schema, compaction details and the full migration story are shortened.

steps.caption: Discord stored messages in a Cassandra cluster that grew from 12 nodes in 2017 to 177 nodes holding trillions of messages by early 2022. Its on-call team was "frequently paged for issues with the database."
Messages are partitioned by channel plus a bucket, "a static time window", so a channel's recent messages sit together.
Hot partitions: "Lots of concurrent reads as users interact with servers can hotspot a partition." Because reads and writes use quorum, latency on those nodes spread to other queries they served.

predict.prompt: A huge server's busiest channel gets a flood of reads. All of that channel's recent messages are in one partition. What happens?

options.text: The load spreads evenly over all nodes
options.explanation: Partitioning by channel puts one channel's load on the same few nodes.

options.text: That partition's nodes get overloaded, and every query touching those nodes slows down
options.explanation: Right. Discord calls it a "hot partition"; with quorum reads, the slowdown spread.
One partition lives on a few nodes, and those have limits.

steps.caption: Discord added data services between the API and the database, with "roughly one gRPC endpoint per database query". They coalesce requests: "If multiple users are requesting the same row at the same time, we'll only query the database once."
Requests are routed by "consistent hash-based routing" on the channel ID, so all requests for one channel meet at the same instance and can be merged.

predict.prompt: Coalescing only works if requests for the same channel reach the same data-service instance. How can that be arranged?

options.text: Route each request by a hash of its channel ID, so one channel always goes to the same instance
options.explanation: Right. Discord uses consistent hash-based routing on the channel ID.

options.text: Send requests to a random instance
options.explanation: Then identical requests land on different instances and can't be merged.

options.text: Use a single instance for everything
options.explanation: That would be a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

steps.caption: Discord moved the messages cluster to ScyllaDB, which is Cassandra-compatible and written in C++, so it has no garbage-collection pauses. A rewritten migrator ran at up to 3.2 million messages a second, cutting the estimate from three months to nine days. The switch happened in May 2022.
Results Discord reports: 177 Cassandra nodes became 72 ScyllaDB nodes, and the slowest 1% of historical message fetches went from 40–125 ms to 15 ms.

quiz.prompt: What problem does partitioning by channel plus a time bucket create, and how did Discord soften it?

options.text: Messages get lost; Discord added backups
options.explanation: Partitioning doesn't lose messages; it concentrates load.

options.text: A very busy channel concentrates load on a few nodes; data services merge identical requests so the database sees fewer
options.explanation: Right. Coalescing turns many identical reads into one.

options.text: It makes writes impossible; Discord switched to files
options.explanation: Writes work; hot reads were the issue.

quiz.prompt: Why does request coalescing need routing by channel ID?

options.text: Identical requests must arrive at the same instance to be merged
options.explanation: Right. Consistent hashing on the channel sends them there.
They're used for routing, not secrecy.
